When writing on the early sections, resist the urge to retell Jane’s suffering. Examiners reward candidates who treat Brontë as an author making choices: why the red room, why Helen’s patience, why Brocklehurst’s hypocrisy? Use Victorian context (charity schools, treatment of dependants, religious hypocrisy) to sharpen, not replace, your close reading.

before.exam_tip_html: Examiners reward candidates who treat the confession chapters as consciously constructed narrative, not just the ‘twist’ being revealed. Track Stevenson’s structural choice to shift narrators: Utterson → Lanyon → Jekyll. Ask why each voice comes at this stage and why the final chapter ends with the narrator’s own death-in-words. Pair this with context about Victorian doubles, hidden vice or addiction.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about Staves 4–5, examiners reward candidates who track the contrast between the two endings Dickens shows: the lonely grave and the joyful family Christmas. Zoom in on small grammatical choices — Scrooge’s imperatives, his similes, his oxymorons — and link them to the moral argument that action (not just feeling) defines redemption.

before.exam_tip_html: A useful rule: never leave a quotation without analysis, and never leave analysis without a link. Examiners want to see joined-up thinking, so end every paragraph with a sentence that pushes back to Dickens’s argument — ‘This shows that Dickens is arguing...’. Without that tie-back, even excellent close reading can plateau at a middle band.
